youtube.title: Why Is Mongolia Trapped Between Just Two Countries?
youtube.description:
Mongolia is bigger than France, Germany, Britain and Italy put together, yet it borders only two countries: Russia and China. Why does Mongolia only border two countries, and what does that mean for its trade, its fuel and its foreign policy?

This video follows the map from Genghis Khan's empire to the 1727 Treaty of Kyakhta, independence in 1911-12, the 1945 plebiscite and the 1962 border treaty, then looks at the mines, railways, pipelines and 'third neighbours' that shape Mongolia's choices today, with both neighbours' positions given.

{CHAPTERS}

tags: why does mongolia only border two countries
youtube.comment: If your country could only have two neighbours, which two would you pick? 👇

sources.claim: Mongolia covers 1.56 million square kilometres
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, Mongolia (area 1,564,116 sq km), 2024 edition

sources.claim: Mongolia borders only Russia and China; 3,452 km with Russia, 4,630 km with China, 8,082 km in total
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, Mongolia, land boundaries, 2024 edition

sources.claim: Russia lies along Mongolia's north and north-west (including Tuva and the Altai Republic); China along the south, east and west
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, Mongolia, 2024 edition; Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia: land

sources.claim: Nearest seaport Tianjin is about 1,700 km by rail from Ulaanbaatar
sources.source: World Bank, Mongolia trade and transport facilitation reports (Tianjin port route), 2020

sources.claim: Kazakhstan comes within about 37 km of Mongolia in the far west
sources.source: Measured on border data (OpenStreetMap / Natural Earth); widely cited figure of about 37 km

sources.claim: About 2,400 km from west to east
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia (about 1,490 miles / 2,400 km east-west)

sources.claim: Bigger than France, Germany, Britain and Italy combined
sources.source: CIA World Factbook areas: France 643,801; Germany 357,022; UK 243,610; Italy 301,340 sq km (total 1,545,773)

sources.claim: Second-largest landlocked country after Kazakhstan
sources.source: CIA World Factbook, country area rankings, 2024

sources.claim: About 3.5 million people, about two per square kilometre, the most sparsely populated country
sources.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, population 2023-24; World Bank population density data, 2023

sources.claim: Almost half live in Ulaanbaatar
sources.source: National Statistics Office of Mongolia, 2023 (about 1.7 million in the capital)

sources.claim: Ulaanbaatar is often called the coldest national capital
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ulaanbaatar; average annual temperature below 0 °C

sources.claim: Russia, China and Mongolia meet at Tavan Bogd
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Altai Mountains / Tavan Bogd

sources.claim: One main railway runs south from Ulaanbaatar to Erenhot; much of the trade moves along it or by truck
sources.source: Ulaanbaatar Railway JSC (Trans-Mongolian line Ulaanbaatar-Zamyn-Üüd-Erenhot); World Bank Mongolia Economic Update, 2022-2023 (rail and road freight at the border crossings)

sources.claim: Mongolia's rails are 1,520 mm apart, China's 1,435 mm; carriages are lifted onto new wheels at Erenhot
sources.source: Ulaanbaatar Railway JSC; China Railway; Trans-Mongolian Railway descriptions

sources.claim: In 2023 about nine in ten dollars of Mongolia's exports went to China
sources.source: Mongolia Customs General Administration, 2023 annual trade data (China about 92% of exports)

sources.claim: Mongolia exported a record 69.6 million tonnes of coal in 2023
sources.source: Mongolia Customs General Administration, January 2024 release; reported by Reuters, January 2024

sources.claim: Most of Mongolia's petrol and diesel comes from Russia
sources.source: Mongolia Customs General Administration import data; Reuters reporting, 2022-2024

sources.claim: In 1206 Temüjin took the title Genghis Khan
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Genghis Khan

sources.claim: Around 1279 the Mongol Empire covered about 24 million square kilometres
sources.source: Rein Taagepera, 'Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities', International Studies Quarterly, 1997

sources.claim: The empire split into rival khanates ruled by different branches of Genghis Khan's family, from about 1260
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongol empire

sources.claim: In 1368 the Mongol (Yuan) rulers of China were driven back to the steppe
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Yuan dynasty

sources.claim: Southern Mongols came under the Qing from 1636; the Khalkha submitted at Dolon Nor in 1691
sources.source: C.R. Bawden, The Modern History of Mongolia (1968); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia: history

sources.claim: Russia and the Qing signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Nerchinsk

sources.claim: The 1727 Treaty of Kyakhta set the Russia-Qing line between Siberia and Mongolia
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Treaty of Kyakhta (1727)

sources.claim: Kyakhta was the main fur-for-tea trading post for over a century; tea caravans crossed the steppe from Kalgan through Urga
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Kyakhta; Martha Avery, The Tea Road: China and Russia Meet Across the Steppe (2003)

sources.claim: Revolution against the Qing broke out in 1911; the last emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Chinese Revolution (1911-12); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Puyi

sources.claim: On 29 December 1911 the Bogd Khan was enthroned as ruler of independent Mongolia
sources.source: C.R. Bawden, The Modern History of Mongolia (1968)

sources.claim: Autonomy in 1915, Chinese troops in 1919, revolution in 1921, People's Republic in 1924
sources.source: Tripartite Treaty of Kyakhta, 1915; Bawden (1968); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia: history

sources.claim: In July 1921 Mongolian revolutionaries and Red Army units took Urga
sources.source: Bawden (1968); Encyclopaedia Britannica, Damdiny Sükhbaatar

sources.claim: The Mongolian People's Republic, declared in 1924, was the world's second communist state, aligned with Moscow
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia: the Mongolian People's Republic

sources.claim: Tuva joined the Soviet Union in 1944
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Tuva

sources.claim: China's government argued that the Qing had ruled Mongolia for two centuries and that it was part of China's inherited territory
sources.source: Provisional Constitution of the Republic of China, 11 March 1912, Article 3 (Mongolia listed as Chinese territory); Bawden (1968)

sources.claim: Yalta, secretly agreed: 'The status quo in Outer-Mongolia (The Mongolian People's Republic) shall be preserved.'
sources.source: Agreement Regarding Entry of the Soviet Union into the War Against Japan, Yalta, 11 February 1945, kept secret until February 1946 (US State Department, Foreign Relations of the United States)

sources.claim: The October 1945 plebiscite was run in Mongolia by the Mongolian authorities, as required by China's 1945 treaty with the USSR, with a Chinese observer present
sources.source: Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance, exchange of notes, 14 August 1945; Bawden (1968)

sources.claim: Official count of the 20 October 1945 vote, reported by the Chinese government: 487,409 for independence, none against
sources.source: Official result reported by the Republic of China, cited in Bawden (1968)

sources.claim: Some historians doubt the count because the vote took place under Soviet influence
sources.source: Bawden (1968); Christopher Atwood, Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire (2004)

sources.claim: The Republic of China recognised Mongolia's independence in January 1946
sources.source: Republic of China government recognition, 5 January 1946; Encyclopaedia Britannica

sources.claim: The China-Mongolia border treaty was signed on 26 December 1962
sources.source: Sino-Mongolian Boundary Treaty, 26 December 1962

sources.claim: About 6.3 million Mongols live in China
sources.source: National Bureau of Statistics of China, Seventh National Census, 2020 (6,290,204)

sources.claim: Mongolia sided with Moscow in the Sino-Soviet split; Soviet troops were based there and left in 1992
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Mongolia: history; Bawden (1968); Russian troop withdrawal completed 1992

sources.claim: Oyu Tolgoi is about 80 km north of the Chinese border; Rio Tinto owns 66%, the Mongolian government 34%
sources.source: Rio Tinto, Oyu Tolgoi project page and Annual Report 2023

sources.claim: The Tavan Tolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway opened in 2022
sources.source: Government of Mongolia / Montsame news agency, September 2022

sources.claim: A cross-border railway from Gashuunsukhait to Ganqimaodu is planned to carry coal into China
sources.source: Mongolia-China intergovernmental agreement on the Gashuunsukhait-Ganqimaodu cross-border railway, 2024 (Montsame; Xinhua)

sources.claim: In 2014 China and Mongolia raised ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership described as mutually beneficial
sources.source: China-Mongolia Joint Declaration, 21 August 2014 (Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs)

sources.claim: After the Dalai Lama's November 2016 visit, China, which calls him a separatist, postponed talks; Mongolia's foreign minister said he would not be invited again during this government's term
sources.source: Reuters, November and December 2016

sources.claim: Russian Railways owns half of Ulaanbaatar Railway
sources.source: Ulaanbaatar Railway JSC (50% Mongolia, 50% Russian Railways)

sources.claim: Putin made an official visit to Ulaanbaatar in September 2024
sources.source: Kremlin, 3 September 2024; Reuters, 3 September 2024

sources.claim: The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023
sources.source: International Criminal Court press release, 17 March 2023

sources.claim: In October 2024 ICC judges found Mongolia failed to arrest him and referred it to the Assembly of States Parties
sources.source: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II decision, 24 October 2024

sources.claim: Mongolia buys 95% of its petroleum products and over 20% of its electricity from its immediate neighbourhood; it has always kept a policy of neutrality
sources.source: Mongolian government spokesperson, quoted by Politico, 2 September 2024

sources.claim: Mongolia says it courts 'third neighbours', including the US, Japan, South Korea, the EU and India; the phrase traced to James Baker's 1990 visit; policy in 1994
sources.source: Concept of Foreign Policy of Mongolia, 1994; US State Department history of US-Mongolia relations

sources.claim: 2019 US-Mongolia strategic partnership
sources.source: Joint Statement on the Strategic Third Neighbor Partnership, The White House, 31 July 2019

sources.claim: Ulaanbaatar and Washington are more than 10,000 km apart
sources.source: Great-circle distance between the two capitals

sources.claim: Power of Siberia 2 would carry up to 50 billion cubic metres a year; about 960 km in Mongolia; the detailed route has not been made public
sources.source: Gazprom, Power of Siberia 2 / Soyuz Vostok project information, 2022-2024

sources.claim: In September 2025 Gazprom said it signed a legally binding memorandum with CNPC; no price was made public
sources.source: Gazprom statement and Reuters, 2 September 2025

sources.claim: Long truck queues at the China-Mongolia border crossings
sources.source: Reuters and World Bank Mongolia Economic Update, 2022-2023

sources.claim: In 2016 China, Russia and Mongolia signed an economic corridor programme for trade and transport links
sources.source: Programme on the Construction of the China-Mongolia-Russia Economic Corridor, Tashkent, 23 June 2016

sources.claim: In May 2023 Macron became the first French president to visit Mongolia, with uranium and critical minerals discussed
sources.source: Élysée Palace, 21 May 2023; Reuters, 21 May 2023

sources.claim: The Wakhan Corridor is a strip of Afghanistan between Tajikistan and Pakistan, drawn to keep two empires apart
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Wakhan Corridor; Anglo-Russian Pamir agreement, 1895
